title: Expedition 33 Damage Mechanics - How Pictos & Lumina Stacking Works
description: How damage actually works in Expedition 33: Attack Power as the baseline, additive vs multiplicative stacking, weapon affinity, Pictos vs Lumina, hidden bonuses, and the Lumina point economy.

sections.title: Damage Starts From Attack Power
sections.content:
Every damage number in Expedition 33 is derived from a single combat stat: Attack Power. Skills, base attacks, free aim shots and counterattacks are all Attack Power run through different coefficients and multipliers.

Here are the baselines that matter, measured against a fixed Attack Power of 1,000:

SourceDamage
Base attack100% of Attack Power (1,000)
Free aim shot15% of Attack Power (150) - an additional bonus applies vs flying enemies
CounterattackRoughly 6x-7.4x Attack Power (sources disagree - see below)
SkillsEach skill has its own multiplier
Weak-point shotNot derived from Attack Power at all - fixed per enemy type and level

Two consequences follow immediately.

Counterattacking is worth far more than it looks

A successful counter carries a multiplier in the region of 6x to 7.4x your Attack Power. That is larger than most early and mid-game skills, and it costs no AP. If you have been dodging rather than parrying purely for safety, the damage maths argues strongly for learning to parry.

Note that two community datamining efforts give different figures for the base counter multiplier - one measured 5.95x and another measured 735% (7.35x), with Gradient Counters at 1029%. We quote the range rather than pick a winner. The exact value is not important to the conclusion; the order of magnitude is.

Weak-point shots do not scale

Weak-point damage appears to be fixed per enemy type and level and does not grow with your Attack Power. This makes it extremely strong in the early game and progressively useless later, to the point where a late-game weak-point hit can be far weaker than simply shooting the enemy elsewhere. Do not build around it.

sections.title: Additive vs Multiplicative - What Actually Stacks
sections.content:
This is the single most misunderstood part of Expedition 33's combat, and a lot of guides get it wrong - including our own first draft of this page. Here is the accurate version.

Many bonuses multiply - but not all of them

A large share of damage bonuses multiply with each other rather than adding up. When two bonuses multiply, the second one is applied to the already-boosted number, so it is worth more than the first:

Scenario (base 1,000 damage)Additive resultMultiplicative result
One +50% bonus1,5001,500
Two +50% bonuses2,0002,250
Three counter bonuses: +25%, +50%, +75%2,500 (2.5x)3,280 (3.28x)

This is why stacking many small bonuses outperforms seeking one huge bonus - and why endgame builds reach damage figures that look impossible.

The important caveat

It is not true that every bonus in the game is multiplicative. Community datamining has found a mix. Some sources multiply, others are additive within their own category, and there are reportedly more additive damage Luminas than multiplicative ones. Any guide that tells you all bonuses are multiplicative is overstating it.

What you can rely on in practice:

  • Damage begins at Attack Power and passes through a chain of modifiers
  • Many of those modifiers multiply - particularly ones tied to different conditions (low HP, Burn, Marked, Stunned, first hit, counter, shield count, and so on)
  • Because the chain multiplies, stacking several different conditions beats stacking several copies of one condition

What this means for your build

When you compare two Pictos, do not simply add their percentages together and compare the total. Prefer bonuses whose conditions differ from what you already have, because those are the ones most likely to multiply into each other rather than sit in the same additive bucket.

A practical rule: two different +25% bonuses from different conditions are usually worth more than one +50% from a condition you have already covered.

sections.title: Weapon Affinity: Why Raw Might Is a Trap
sections.content:
Attack Power is not driven by the Might attribute directly. It is driven by weapon affinity - the letter grades shown next to each weapon.

Every weapon displays affinity letters against certain attributes. Investing in an attribute the weapon has high affinity with raises Attack Power considerably more than investing in Might.

AffinityEffect of investing in that attribute
SHighest gain (only appears at maximum weapon level)
AVery high gain
BHigh gain - generally still beats Might
C / DModest gain
No letterLowest gain

A worked comparison

With Maelle and the Medalum weapon, the same character at the same level produces meaningfully different Attack Power depending purely on where the points go:

  • All points into Might - roughly 5,800 Attack Power
  • All points into Defense (the weapon's affinity stat) - roughly 7,100 Attack Power, plus higher Defense and critical rate as a side effect

That is a gain of around 22% to Attack Power from respecting alone, with defensive stats thrown in for free.

Weapon level raises affinity

Upgrading a weapon does not only increase its raw damage - it raises the affinity grade. This means a weapon upgrade improves your damage twice over: once directly, and once by making your existing attribute investment more efficient.

Do not stay locked in

Respec items (recall tints) are cheap and available at any flag or camp. If you find a better weapon with different affinity, respec immediately rather than carrying mismatched attributes. Building your attributes around your weapon is the correct order of operations - not the other way round.

sections.title: Pictos vs Lumina: What Each One Actually Gives You
sections.content:
Pictos and Lumina are two halves of the same system, and confusing them is the most common early mistake.

PictosLumina
Slots per character3Limited by Lumina Points
Grants stat bonusesYesNo
Grants the passive effectYesYes
Usable by several characters at onceNoYes
Consumes Lumina PointsNoYes

How Lumina is unlocked

  • Equip a Pictos and win 4 battles - its Lumina becomes Mastered
  • Mastery is tracked by the Pictos, not the character. You can split those 4 battles across different party members and it still counts
  • Each Pictos can only ever produce one Lumina
  • A character cannot equip a Pictos and its same-named Lumina at the same time - there is no double-dipping

The key distinction

A Pictos gives you stats plus the effect. A Lumina gives you only the effect. This is why higher-level Pictos are valuable even when you already own the effect: the effect is identical between tiers, but the stat bonuses are not.

So the correct way to think about it: choose your three equipped Pictos primarily for the stats they provide, and use Lumina Points to spread the effects you need across the rest of the party.

sections.title: The Lumina Point Economy
sections.content:
Lumina effects cost Lumina Points, ranging from as little as 1 point up to around 40. Points come from two sources:

  • +1 per level up, for each character
  • Colour of Lumina consumables, redeemed with the Curator at camp

The trick that saves the most points

Because expensive Luminas cost a lot of points, but a Pictos slot costs nothing but a slot, there is an obvious optimisation most players miss:

If a Lumina is expensive, equip the Pictos instead of buying the Lumina. You get the identical passive effect for zero Lumina Points, spending only one of that character's three Pictos slots. This works for exactly one character, since only one copy of each Pictos exists - everyone else still has to pay the points if they want the effect.

Conversely, spend your Lumina Points on cheap effects, and hold expensive ones as Pictos. That single swap can free up a large portion of a character's point budget.

Tiered effects stack across tiers

Some effects exist in multiple tiers (I, II, III). You cannot equip the same Lumina twice, but you can stack different tiers of the same effect. A tier II effect typically costs more than tier I while doing the same thing - the point of the higher tier is only that it lets you stack the effect further if you own both.

If you do not need to stack the effect, equip the cheapest tier. If you do, equipping tier I and tier II together is the only way to reach the doubled effect.

Spread points across the party

Resist the urge to dump every Colour of Lumina into one damage dealer. The game repeatedly forces party switches and reserve-team encounters, and a character with no Lumina budget contributes very little.

sections.title: Counterattacks and Free Aim
sections.content:
Both of these damage sources sit outside the normal skill rotation, and both are commonly undervalued.

Counterattacks

Parrying every hit from an enemy triggers a Counterattack, which both negates the incoming damage and deals a large fixed multiplier of your Attack Power. As noted above, community measurements put the counter multiplier between roughly 5.95x and 7.35x, with Gradient Counters substantially higher again.

There is also a dedicated category of Luminas that exist purely to push counter damage higher - notably the Augmented Counter line. If you parry reliably, these are among the most efficient damage per Lumina Point in the game.

Gradient Counters are triggered by parrying Gradient Attacks specifically, and use the dash input rather than the standard parry input.

Free aim

A free aim shot deals 15% of your Attack Power against normal enemies, with an additional bonus against flying enemies. That is a low per-shot number, but free aim costs no AP and can be fired outside your turn, which makes it useful for finishing low-health targets, breaking bars, and applying weapon-based effects.

Because free aim scales directly with Attack Power, it benefits from the exact same stacking and affinity advice as everything else - unlike weak-point shots, which do not scale at all.

sections.title: Hidden Bonuses Not Shown in Your Stats
sections.content:
Community datamining has identified several bonuses that are not displayed anywhere in the game's UI. They simply apply.

The Pictos reported to carry hidden damage bonuses are:

PictosReported hidden bonus
Sweet KillApproximately +10% damage, not shown
Dead Energy IIApproximately +10% damage, not shown
First StrikeApproximately +10% damage, not shown, lasting the whole battle
TeamworkApproximately +11% damage on top of its displayed +10%

Two cautions apply. First, whether these hidden bonuses stack additively or multiplicatively with each other has not been settled. Second, because they are undocumented, they may be corrected in a future patch.

There is also at least one community report of a weapon carrying an unlisted damage bonus. That claim is less well corroborated than the Pictos list above, so we are not naming a specific weapon for it.

sections.title: Worked Example: 800K to 15M
sections.content:
To show how much of your damage comes purely from getting the stacking right rather than from raw stats, here is a like-for-like comparison:

SetupResult
Maelle, Medalum, Virtuose Stance, no damage Luminas~800,000 damage
Identical setup, plus ~200 Lumina Points of damage bonuses~15,000,000 damage

Same character. Same weapon. Same level. Same skill. Same execution. No critical hit in either case. The only change is the presence of roughly 200 points worth of damage bonuses - and the damage goes up by a factor of about 19.

This is not a cheese build. It is what happens when a chain of multipliers compounds instead of adding up, and it is why replaying the same fight with the same stats can produce completely different results once you fix your Pictos and Lumina layout.

The practical sequence to follow:

  • Set attributes according to your weapon's affinity, not raw Might
  • Upgrade the weapon to raise affinity grades
  • Fill the three Pictos slots for the stats they give
  • Spend Lumina Points on cheap effects, and hold expensive effects as Pictos instead
  • Prefer bonuses from different conditions so they multiply rather than sit in one additive bucket

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
• Adding percentages together. Many bonuses multiply. Two +50% bonuses are not +100%; they are +125% or more, depending on which category each falls into.
  • Maxing Might. Attack Power comes from weapon affinity attributes. Might is usually the wrong place for your points.
  • Buying expensive Luminas with points. Equip the Pictos instead and keep the points for cheap effects.
  • Trusting the in-game damage tags. The low / medium / high / very high / extreme labels appear to be derived from base scaling multiplied by hit count, and they ignore conditional effects entirely. A low-damage tag on a multi-hit skill with a big conditional multiplier can comfortably outdamage a high-damage tag.
  • Assuming every bonus is multiplicative. It is a mix. This is the single most repeated error in existing Expedition 33 guides - including ours until it was corrected.
  • Building around weak-point shots. They are fixed damage and do not scale with your build.
  • Skipping weapon upgrades. Weapon level raises affinity grade, which makes your attribute investment more efficient as well as raising raw damage.
